tagline: An old inn and a converted stable trace Marshall’s traveling life.
intro: Michigan Avenue carries Marshall’s I-94 business loop through downtown, where the historic district includes homes, civic buildings and commercial blocks. The district became a National Historic Landmark in 1991. Along West Michigan Avenue, a former livery stable serves as city hall, while Wagner’s Block has a slate-covered mansard roof with oval windows.

The National House prospered as a stop on the Territorial Road to Detroit after its construction in 1835. In 1857, William Prindle began a stagecoach stop and livery stable; carriage and wagon shops occupied its upper floor. By the late 1920s the building held an automobile garage and service station, before a preservation project turned it into the town hall in 1930.

From the National House on South Parkview, an eastward trip along West Michigan Avenue reaches the former stable at number 323, then Wagner’s Block at number 143. The surrounding district’s rectangular street grid contains Greek Revival, Italianate and Gothic Revival buildings.

moments.title: Fountain Circle
moments.text: The National House faces Parkview and the old Courthouse Square, a brick inn whose uses have changed repeatedly since the Territorial Road brought travelers through Marshall. Completed in 1835, it opened with a formal ball on New Year’s Day, 1836. Hotel operations ended in 1879; the building later housed wagon and windmill manufacturing, then apartments. New owners refurbished it and reopened the National House Inn in 1977. Its two-story brick walls stand on a sandstone foundation. Five upper-floor windows cross the main facade, with plain stone lintels above the openings and a gabled roof overhead.

moments.title: Honolulu House
moments.text: A pagoda-roofed tower rises above the entrance stairs of Honolulu House, with a wide veranda below. Abner Pratt, a former Michigan Supreme Court chief justice and U.S. consul to Hawaii, built the house in 1860 after living in the islands. Its Hawaiian inspiration joined Italianate and Gothic Revival styles. Ornamental columns support the veranda, linked by arches of wooden tracery. The Marshall Historical Society acquired the house in 1961 for a museum. White board-and-batten siding covers the two-story house, and large bay windows mark each end, beneath a roof with four symmetrically placed chimneys.

moments.title: Governor's Mansion
moments.text: Marshall’s confidence that it would become Michigan’s capital went as far as building a Governor’s Mansion. Lansing was chosen instead in 1847.
